strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: improving spatial and spatio-temporal reasoning in VLMs from monocular RGB video without requiring depth sensors or prebuilt 3D maps.

The proposed system is practically motivated and conceptually sensible: using a frozen CUT3R-style reconstruction encoder to provide geometry and camera tokens, then fusing them with standard visual tokens inside a LLaVA-Video-style model.

The work contributes both model and data resources: over 200K automatically generated spatial instruction QA pairs and a new VSTemporalI-Bench with 138.6K QA pairs covering camera dynamics, camera-object relations, and object-object relative position.

Empirical results are strong on the reported benchmarks. VLM-3R substantially improves over open-source and proprietary baselines on VSI-Bench, especially for distance, size, direction, and route-planning tasks, and also leads on the proposed VSTemporalI-Bench.

The ablation on VSI-Bench is useful: compared with a fine-tuned LLaVA-NeXT-Video baseline trained on the same spatial instruction data, the full model improves average performance from 57.74 to 60.90, and removing camera or geometry tokens generally reduces performance.

The appendix provides useful implementation details, including base model, visual tower, LoRA configuration, frozen modules, training hardware, and task-generation logic, which improves reproducibility.
weaknesses: The evidence does not fully disentangle the contribution of the architecture from the contribution of task-specific generated training data. The large gap over many baselines may largely reflect supervised fine-tuning on similarly structured spatial QA data, while the architecture-only gain over the fine-tuned LLaVA-NeXT-Video baseline on VSI-Bench is modest.

The VSTemporalI-Bench comparison appears less controlled: VLM-3R is fine-tuned on the VSTI training split, but the table mainly compares against off-the-shelf proprietary and open-source VLMs. A fine-tuned LLaVA-NeXT-Video baseline and ablations on VSTI are needed to support the claim that geometry/camera token fusion, rather than benchmark-specific training, drives the gains.

The new temporal benchmark is narrower than the name suggests. The manuscript explicitly states that all current VSTemporalI-Bench tasks use static environments and camera motion only, with independently moving objects left to future work. This limits claims about dynamic 3D temporal reasoning.

The benchmark and training data are automatically generated from 3D metadata using templates. This enables scale, but also raises concerns about template bias, shortcut learning, answer-distribution artifacts, and limited linguistic diversity. The paper does not provide enough human validation, noise analysis, or robustness checks for these generated QA labels.

There is potential overlap or distribution coupling between training data, evaluation tasks, and source datasets such as ScanNet, ScanNet++, and ARKitScenes. The paper should more clearly document scene-level splits and ensure that no scenes or near-duplicate trajectories leak between train and test, especially for the newly introduced benchmark.

Some claims are overstated. The method is described as end-to-end and not relying on reconstruction, but it depends heavily on a pretrained frozen CUT3R reconstruction model and its latent geometry/pose tokens. This is still a learned reconstruction module, even if explicit maps are not constructed at inference time.

The ablations are incomplete. There is no clear comparison to using CUT3R outputs in simpler ways, no evaluation of sensitivity to reconstruction quality, no runtime/memory analysis, and no study of how performance scales with number of frames or failure cases such as textureless scenes, fast camera motion, or non-rigid/dynamic content.

Reproducibility remains only partial. Training details are given, but the manuscript does not clearly state whether code, generated data, benchmark splits, and evaluation scripts will be released; the project website field appears blank in the extracted manuscript. Without these, reproducing the benchmark and results would be difficult.

Presentation has several polish issues, including inconsistent benchmark naming (VSTemporalI-Bench/VSTI-Bench/VS TemporalI-Bench), typos, and occasional imprecise wording. These are secondary to the experimental concerns but reduce clarity.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: spatial and temporal reasoning from ordinary monocular video, avoiding explicit depth sensors or prebuilt 3D maps at inference time.

The proposed system is conceptually reasonable: frozen CUT3R-style reconstructive tokens, camera/view tokens, visual tokens, and a lightweight fusion module on top of a video LMM are plausible ingredients for improving 3D-aware VQA.

The work includes a substantial data-generation effort, with over 200K spatial QA pairs and a large VSTemporalI-Bench benchmark. The task taxonomy is clear and covers useful capabilities such as camera displacement, camera-object distance, and relative object position.

The reported results show sizeable improvements over many off-the-shelf VLMs on VSI-Bench and VSTemporalI-Bench, and the ablation against a fine-tuned LLaVA-NeXT-Video baseline suggests the 3D tokens add some value beyond data alone.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is a major concern. VLM-3R is fine-tuned on task-specific generated data, including the VSTemporalI-Bench training split, while most compared proprietary and open-source models appear to be evaluated without comparable fine-tuning. This makes the headline comparisons to GPT-4o, Gemini, and larger open-source models difficult to interpret as evidence of a generally stronger model.

The gains attributable to the core architecture are much smaller than the headline tables imply. On VSI-Bench, the full model improves only from 57.74 to 60.90 over a fine-tuned LLaVA-NeXT-Video baseline trained on the same 200K data. Several component ablations differ by only 1-3 points, and some tasks degrade, so the architectural contribution is modest relative to the claims.

There is insufficient evidence against data leakage or benchmark overfitting. The training data is generated from ScanNet, ScanNet++, and ARKitScenes using task logic similar to VSI-Bench, but the paper does not clearly specify scene-level splits, overlap checks, or whether templated questions and object distributions leak between training and evaluation.

The new VSTemporalI-Bench is less compelling than claimed as a temporal benchmark. The paper states that all current tasks use static environments and only camera motion; there are no independently moving objects. Several tasks can be solved from camera poses and static scene geometry rather than requiring rich video temporal understanding.

The benchmark labels are generated from ground-truth geometry, poses, depth, and annotations, while the model input is RGB video. This is acceptable in principle, but the paper does not sufficiently analyze annotation noise, reconstruction failure modes, tolerance sensitivity for numerical answers, or whether the questions are visually answerable from the sampled frames.

The method is not technically very original: it largely combines an existing reconstruction model, an existing video LMM, LoRA fine-tuning, and a standard cross-attention fusion block. The paper's novelty rests heavily on data curation and integration, but those components are described at a high level and not validated deeply.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives some training hyperparameters, but lacks enough detail about data release status, exact scene splits, prompt templates, frame sampling, preprocessing scripts, answer parsing, and evaluation settings to reproduce the central results with confidence.

The presentation overstates conclusions. Phrases such as robust spatial reasoning, state-of-the-art performance, and human-like spatial intelligence are not fully supported by the limited indoor-scene evaluation, static temporal setup, and unfair baseline comparison protocol.

strengths: Timely and useful problem setting: improving 3D spatial and spatial-temporal reasoning from monocular video without requiring depth sensors or pre-built maps is important for embodied AI, robotics, AR, and video LMMs.

The proposed architecture is technically sensible: using a frozen CUT3R-style spatial encoder to provide geometry and camera-view tokens, then fusing these with native visual tokens through cross-attention, is a clean way to inject 3D priors into an existing video LMM.

Empirical gains are large on the reported benchmarks. VLM-3R improves VSI-Bench average performance substantially over LLaVA-NeXT-Video-7B and other open models, and also reports strong results on the new VSTemporalI-Bench, including gains on camera displacement, movement direction, and camera-object relations.

The ablation study is useful and reasonably targeted. Comparing the full model against variants without geometry tokens, without camera tokens, and against a fine-tuned LLaVA-NeXT-Video baseline supports the claim that the spatial components contribute beyond instruction-tuning alone.

The paper contributes not only a model but also scalable spatial QA generation and a large visual-spatial-temporal benchmark. The task taxonomy is well motivated and covers both frame-level and sequence-level spatial reasoning.

Reproducibility is better than average for a method paper: the manuscript gives the base model, visual tower, spatial tower, LoRA settings, training duration/hardware, optimizer settings, and dataset/task distributions.
weaknesses: The strongest concern is evaluation fairness and possible data/task leakage. The training data is automatically generated from ScanNet, ScanNet++, and ARKitScenes using VSI-like task logic, while evaluation is on VSI-Bench and a new benchmark generated from similar sources and templates. The paper does not clearly establish scene-level separation, template separation, or dataset overlap controls, so some gains may reflect task-format adaptation rather than general spatial reasoning.

The comparison to many baselines is not fully controlled. VLM-3R is fine-tuned on large task-specific spatial QA data, and on VSTemporalI-Bench it is fine-tuned on the benchmark training split, while many API/open-source baselines appear to be evaluated zero-shot. This supports usefulness, but weakens claims of architectural superiority over similarly fine-tuned alternatives.

The new VSTemporalI-Bench is valuable, but currently limited: all environments are static and temporal reasoning comes from camera motion only. This is acknowledged, but it means the benchmark does not yet test independently moving objects or richer 4D scene dynamics implied by the broader motivation.

The architectural novelty is moderate. The main modeling idea is to reuse a strong pretrained reconstruction model and fuse its latent tokens into an LMM; this is practical and effective, but less conceptually novel than the framing sometimes suggests.

The paper relies heavily on automatically generated numerical and multiple-choice QA. More qualitative error analysis, calibration analysis for metric estimates, and evaluation on out-of-distribution real monocular videos would strengthen the evidence that the model has robust spatial understanding rather than dataset-specific QA competence.

Some presentation issues reduce clarity: terminology alternates between VSTemporalI-Bench and VSTI-Bench, some claims such as “state-of-the-art” are broad relative to the controlled evidence, and details about benchmark release, exact splits, and baseline prompting/evaluation protocols are not sufficiently explicit.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: spatial and temporal reasoning from monocular video for VLMs, without requiring depth sensors or pre-built 3D maps at inference.
weaknesses: The method is somewhat incremental architecturally. The core model mainly combines a frozen video VLM, a frozen CUT3R geometry encoder, cross-attention fusion, and LoRA instruction tuning. This is sensible and useful, but the novelty is more in integration and data/benchmark construction than in a fundamentally new modeling idea.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: improving monocular-video VLMs for 3D spatial and spatio-temporal reasoning without requiring depth sensors or prebuilt explicit 3D maps at inference.

The proposed data pipeline is potentially useful. The manuscript describes more than 200K generated spatial QA pairs, 4,225 route-planning examples, and a new VSTI-Bench with 138.6K QA pairs spanning camera displacement, camera movement direction, camera-object distance, camera-object relative distance, and object-object relative position.

The empirical section covers several relevant benchmarks. VLM-3R improves over its finetuned LLaVA-NeXT-Video baseline on VSI-Bench, especially on relative direction, room size, absolute distance, and route planning, and also reports competitive results on ScanQA/SQA3D and OST-Bench.
The method is technically plausible: using CUT3R latent geometry/view tokens and cross-attention fusion with visual tokens is a reasonable way to inject metric-scale geometric priors into a VLM.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty appears limited. The method is largely a combination of an existing video VLM, an existing monocular reconstruction model, LoRA tuning, and a standard cross-attention fusion block. The paper’s own related work notes very similar geometry-token VLMs such as Spatial-MLLM and VG-LLM; the main distinction seems to be replacing normalized-scale geometry with CUT3R metric-scale tokens, which is useful but incremental.

The key ablation evidence is not strong enough for the claims. On VSI-Bench, the full model improves from 57.74 to 60.90 over a finetuned LLaVA-NeXT-Video baseline trained on the same spatial QA data. Removing spatial tokens gives 59.46 and removing view tokens gives 59.09, so the architectural contribution beyond data fine-tuning is modest. The text also contains an apparent inconsistency, claiming the w/o view-token score drops to 50.09 while Table 6 reports 59.09.

The evaluation of the proposed VSTI-Bench is potentially unfair or under-specified. The benchmark includes a large training split, but the paper does not clearly state whether VLM-3R is trained on VSTI training data while many compared proprietary/open-source models are evaluated without comparable training. If so, the large VSTI gains do not establish general superiority in temporal reasoning.

The new temporal benchmark has limited ecological validity. It is generated from static indoor scenes using ground-truth poses, 3D boxes, depth, and instance annotations; all motion is camera motion. This tests camera-centric geometric bookkeeping more than general spatio-temporal reasoning in dynamic environments, despite broad claims about temporal 3D context changes and embodied reasoning.

There is a risk of benchmark/data coupling. Training and evaluation are both derived from ScanNet, ScanNet++, ARKitScenes, and VSI-style templates. Although the paper says standard train/test splits are respected, the generated questions, labels, and task templates are closely matched to the evaluation benchmarks, making it difficult to separate genuine model generalization from task-specific adaptation.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details of QA generation, filtering thresholds, fuzzy matching, prompts, frame sampling, candidate selection, and full training/evaluation protocols are either deferred to supplementary-level descriptions or not specified precisely enough to reproduce the benchmark and results. Code/data availability is not established in the manuscript.

Some claims are overstated relative to evidence. The paper repeatedly describes robust spatial-temporal reasoning and monocular spatial assistance, but the strongest comparisons are mostly against models not trained on the same generated data, and general video/image performance slightly drops versus the base model unless mixed with additional general video data.

Presentation quality is uneven, with typos, inconsistent naming of VSTI/VSTemporalI-Bench, duplicated or awkward phrasing, and table/text inconsistencies. These are not the main reason for rejection, but they reduce confidence in the care of the experimental reporting.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: improving spatial and spatio-temporal reasoning in video VLMs from monocular RGB input, without requiring depth sensors or pre-built 3D maps at inference time.

The proposed system is technically plausible and well motivated. Using a frozen metric-scale reconstruction model (CUT3R) to provide spatial and view tokens, then fusing them with visual tokens through cross-attention, is a clean way to inject geometry while preserving compatibility with an existing VLM backbone.

The empirical results are broadly supportive. VLM-3R achieves the best open-source average on VSI-Bench, with clear gains over the fine-tuned LLaVA-NeXT-Video baseline, especially on geometry-heavy tasks such as relative direction, room size, route planning, and absolute distance.

The new VSTI-Bench is a useful contribution: its five task families explicitly evaluate camera motion, camera-object relations, and frame-dependent object-object relations, which are under-tested in many current video VLM evaluations.

The evaluation is fairly broad, covering VSI-Bench, the proposed VSTI-Bench, ScanQA, SQA3D, OST-Bench, Video-MME, VQA v2, and OpenEQA in the supplement. This helps show that the method is not only overfit to a single spatial QA benchmark.

The paper includes meaningful ablations comparing spatial/view tokens, 2D-2D fusion, explicit point fusion, and different geometry encoders. These support the claim that implicit 3D tokens and metric-scale reconstruction features are beneficial.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is moderate. The main method combines an existing video VLM with an existing feed-forward 3D reconstruction model using a relatively standard cross-attention fusion block. The contribution is valuable, but more engineering-and-integration oriented than a fundamentally new modeling idea.

The strongest gain over the properly fine-tuned baseline on VSI-Bench is modest in aggregate: 60.9 versus 57.7 average. The ablation table also shows relatively small drops when removing spatial or view tokens, suggesting that a significant portion of the improvement may come from the curated training data rather than the proposed fusion mechanism alone.

The VSTI-Bench evaluation is promising but has limitations. The benchmark is automatically generated from static indoor 3D datasets, so all temporal change comes from camera motion rather than dynamic objects or actions. This narrows the claim of temporal reasoning and leaves open whether the model handles real 4D scene dynamics.

There is some risk of benchmark-training entanglement. The paper states that VSTI-Bench has train/test splits and that training/evaluation follow source dataset splits, but it is not fully clear how close the generated training QA templates and test QA templates are, or whether models can exploit templatic regularities rather than robust perception.

The comparison to proprietary models is informative but not always controlled for input protocol, frame sampling, prompting, or answer parsing details. These details matter substantially for video QA and numerical-answer evaluation.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone. The paper gives useful training hyperparameters, but code/data release status, exact QA generation scripts, filtering thresholds, evaluation prompts, frame sampling policy, and answer normalization rules are not sufficiently specified for straightforward reproduction.

Some presentation inconsistencies reduce confidence. For example, the text discussing the ablation says removing view tokens drops performance to 50.09, while Table 6 reports 59.09. The benchmark is also referred to with inconsistent names such as VSTI-Bench and VSTemporalI-Bench.

The method depends on the quality, domain coverage, and metric-scale reliability of CUT3R. The paper acknowledges reconstruction limitations, but does not deeply analyze failure cases under poor camera motion, textureless regions, outdoor scenes, dynamic objects, or scale errors.
